text: The study of cosmic rays offers a unique window into the most energetic processes in the universe. These particles, arriving from the depths of space, carry information about supernova explosions, pulsars, and the very fabric of interstellar space. My research at Cambridge under the guidance of C.V. Raman at IISc and later with P.M.S. Blackett focused on understanding the variation of cosmic ray intensity with geomagnetic latitude. We discovered that cosmic ray intensity shows a pronounced latitude effect, with the intensity at the equator being significantly lower than at higher latitudes. This is because the Earth's magnetic field deflects lower-energy cosmic rays away from the equatorial region, creating a natural spectrometer that allows us to study the energy spectrum of primary cosmic rays.
source: Vikram Sarabhai, PhD Thesis Summary, Cambridge University, 1947

text: Our systematic study of cosmic ray intensity variations at tropical latitudes has revealed several important phenomena. The diurnal variation of cosmic ray intensity — the regular daily fluctuation — is related to the rotation of the Earth through the interplanetary magnetic field. By establishing a network of cosmic ray monitoring stations across India, we have been able to map these variations with unprecedented precision. The data suggests that solar activity has a profound influence on the intensity of galactic cosmic rays reaching Earth, with the eleven-year solar cycle producing a corresponding cycle in cosmic ray intensity. This inverse correlation between solar activity and cosmic ray intensity is now well established and has implications for our understanding of the heliosphere.
source: Vikram Sarabhai, Physical Research Laboratory Annual Report, 1953

text: The Physical Research Laboratory in Ahmedabad was established with the conviction that fundamental research in physics is not a luxury for a developing country, but a necessity. When I founded PRL in 1947, India had just gained independence. There were those who argued that all resources should be directed towards immediate economic needs. I disagreed. A nation without a strong foundation in basic science will always be dependent on others for its technology. PRL was designed to be a centre of excellence in cosmic ray physics, space science, and allied disciplines. It has since grown into one of India's premier research institutions, producing world-class work in astronomy, planetary science, and geosciences.

The phenomenon of the Forbush decrease — the sudden drop in cosmic ray intensity following a solar flare — provides crucial evidence for the interaction between the solar wind and galactic cosmic rays. Our observations at PRL have documented numerous such events, and our analysis indicates that the decrease is caused by the magnetic field carried by the ejected solar plasma, which sweeps away the lower-energy galactic cosmic rays. By studying the onset, duration, and recovery of Forbush decreases at our equatorial station, we can infer properties of the interplanetary magnetic field that are difficult to measure directly. This work contributes to the emerging field of space physics and has practical implications for understanding the space environment through which our future satellites will operate.
source: Vikram Sarabhai, Proceedings of the Indian Academy of Sciences, 1955

text: Our research programme in cosmic ray physics has evolved naturally into space research. The same instruments and techniques that we developed to study cosmic rays from the ground — Geiger counters, cloud chambers, photographic emulsions — can be placed on sounding rockets to make measurements above the atmosphere, where the primary cosmic rays have not yet been modified by atmospheric interactions. This is why the transition from ground-based cosmic ray research to rocket-based space science was such a natural progression for PRL and for India. The skills, the knowledge, and the scientific culture that we built through two decades of cosmic ray research prepared us for the space age.
source: Vikram Sarabhai, Lecture on the Evolution of Space Research in India, 1968

text: The study of geomagnetism at equatorial latitudes is of particular interest because of the phenomenon known as the equatorial electrojet — a narrow band of enhanced electric current flowing in the ionosphere along the magnetic equator. India's geographic position makes it uniquely suited for studying this phenomenon. Our magnetometer stations have recorded detailed data on the daily variation of the geomagnetic field, the effects of solar eclipses on the ionosphere, and the behaviour of magnetic storms at equatorial latitudes. This research is not merely academic; understanding the behaviour of the ionosphere and the geomagnetic field is essential for radio communication, navigation, and the operation of future satellite systems.
source: Vikram Sarabhai, Research Paper on Equatorial Geomagnetism, 1958

text: The upper atmosphere of the Earth is a complex and dynamic system, shaped by solar radiation, the geomagnetic field, and the interaction between the solar wind and the magnetosphere. Our sounding rocket experiments from Thumba have provided valuable data on the composition, temperature, and dynamics of the upper atmosphere at equatorial latitudes. The sodium vapour release experiments, in particular, have allowed us to measure wind speeds and directions at altitudes between 80 and 200 kilometres, revealing complex patterns of atmospheric circulation that were previously unknown. These measurements contribute to global efforts to understand the atmosphere and will be essential for the design and operation of future satellites.
source: Vikram Sarabhai, Report on Upper Atmosphere Research, 1966

text: The design and development of scientific instruments is an art as much as a science. At PRL, we have always emphasised the importance of building our own instruments rather than simply purchasing them from abroad. When we build an instrument ourselves, we understand it at the deepest level. We know its strengths and its limitations. We can modify it, improve it, and adapt it to our specific research needs. This philosophy has served us well. Our cosmic ray telescopes, our magnetometers, our rocket-borne spectrometers — all have been designed and built by our own scientists and engineers, often with capabilities that exceed commercially available alternatives.
source: Vikram Sarabhai, PRL Instrumentation Laboratory Dedication, 1963

text: The theory of solar modulation of cosmic rays, which we have developed over two decades of systematic observation, suggests that the Sun's magnetic field, carried outward by the solar wind, creates a cavity — the heliosphere — within which the intensity of galactic cosmic rays is reduced. As solar activity increases, the magnetic field strengthens, and cosmic ray intensity decreases. This anti-correlation is now established beyond doubt by our long-term monitoring at PRL. The implications extend beyond physics: the variation in cosmic radiation reaching Earth's atmosphere may influence cloud formation and, by extension, climate. This is a hypothesis that future research must investigate rigorously.
source: Vikram Sarabhai, Review Paper on Solar-Cosmic Ray Relations, 1960

text: Scientific research is fundamentally an act of faith in the future. When a young scientist embarks on a new line of investigation, there is no guarantee of success. The results may take years to materialise, and they may not be what was expected. But this uncertainty is not a weakness of science — it is its greatest strength. It is precisely because we do not know in advance what we will discover that research is so valuable. The history of science is filled with examples of seemingly impractical research that led to transformative applications. Cosmic ray research, for instance, has contributed to our understanding of elementary particles, the Sun, the galaxy, and the very nature of matter. These discoveries were not planned — they were the natural outcome of rigorous, curious, open-minded inquiry.
source: Vikram Sarabhai, Convocation Address at Gujarat University, 1964
